is
a fundamental
Breadth-First Search (BFS)

algorithm used to traverse a
tree in a
level-wise manner.
In this
method, nodes are visited one level at a time, starting from the root node, then moving on to all nodes at the next level,
and so on until every node in the tree has been visited.
The traversal begins at the root node, which is the topmost node in the tree. From the root, the algorithm first visits all

immediate child nodes. Once all nodes at
the current
level are processed,
the traversal continues to the nodes at
the
next level. This process continues level by level until all nodes have been visited.
BFS is implemented using a queue data structure, which follows
the First-In-First-Out
(FIFO) principle. At
the
beginning of the traversal, the root node is inserted into the queue. Then, in a loop, the node at the front of the queue is
removed (dequeued), processed, and its children are added (enqueued) to the end of the queue. This ensures that nodes
are processed in the exact order they appear level by level in the tree.
One of the key benefits of BFS in trees is that it does not require tracking visited nodes, because in a tree, each node
is unique and there are no repeated connections or cycles. This makes BFS implementation in trees simpler and more
efficient compared to other structures.
The time complexity of BFS in a tree is O(n), where n is the number of nodes in the tree. This is because each node is
visited exactly once. The space complexity is also O(n) in the worst case, especially when the tree is wide and a large
number of nodes need to be stored in the queue at the same time (for example, all nodes at the bottom level).
